Data loading, exploration and preparation¶

The goal of the project is to forecast the monthly mean sunspot number.

This notebook loads the data, checks that it is clean, explores it and prepares the windows that the models of the next notebooks are trained on. The exploration, more than being descriptive, also backs the choices I make in section 5, such as the scaling and the window length.

1. Setup¶

The functions that the next notebooks also need (loading, split, scaling and windows) live in src/data.py, so every notebook works with exactly the same data. This notebook explains and checks each of them where it is used.

In [1]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from src.data import load_sunspots, make_scaler, make_windows, split_bounds, to_sunspots
from src.style import apply_style
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import acf, pacf

# Set this to True for a palette that stays readable with color vision deficiencies.
PALETTE = apply_style(colorblind_safe=False)

2. Loading¶

The dataset comes from a public CSV file on GitHub (DATA_URL in src/data.py). In this case, I kept a local copy in data/, so the notebook runs without an internet connection and every run sees exactly the same data, even if the remote file changes. If the local copy is missing, it is downloaded again from the original URL.

3. Integrity checks¶

Before looking at the data, I will check that it is what I expect. The sliding windows of section 5 assume that consecutive rows are exactly one month apart: if a month were missing for some reason, a window of 12 rows would silently cover 13 months and nothing would raise an error. I will also check for duplicated months, missing values and negative values, which would make no sense for a count of sunspots.

In [3]:
full_range = pd.date_range(df.index.min(), df.index.max(), freq="MS")

checks = pd.Series({
    "rows": len(df),
    "first month": df.index.min().strftime("%Y-%m"),
    "last month": df.index.max().strftime("%Y-%m"),
    "expected months in range": len(full_range),
    "sorted by time": df.index.is_monotonic_increasing,
    "missing months": len(full_range.difference(df.index)),
    "duplicated months": df.index.duplicated().sum(),
    "missing values": df["Sunspots"].isna().sum(),
    "negative values": (df["Sunspots"] < 0).sum(),
    "months with zero sunspots": (df["Sunspots"] == 0).sum(),
})
checks
Out[3]:
rows                            2820

expected months in range        2820
sorted by time                  True
missing months                     0
duplicated months                  0
missing values                     0
negative values                    0
months with zero sunspots         67
dtype: object

Findings:

The series has 2820 consecutive values, from January 1749 to December 1983 (235 years), sorted, with no gaps, no duplicates, no missing values and no negative values, so no cleaning is needed. There are 67 months with exactly zero sunspots. However, they are not errors since the Sun can go a whole month without visible spots near the minimum of its cycle. They matter later for two main reasons: a log transformation would need log1p instead of log ($\log{0}$ is undefined), and percentage errors such as MAPE are undefined when the true value is zero, so I will not use them.

In [4]:
# Make the monthly spacing explicit in the index.
# In this case, I will add an additional assert because the method asfreq
# would insert a NaN row for any missing month, so I'm asserting that nothing is added.

df = df.asfreq("MS")
assert len(df) == len(full_range) and df["Sunspots"].notna().all()
df.index.freq

4. Visualization¶

4.1 The full series¶

I plot the whole series first to see its overall structure, and then zoom in on the last 34 years to see the month-to-month behavior that the full view surely hides.

In [5]:
sunspots = df["Sunspots"]
zoomed = sunspots["1950":"1983"]

# Centered mean over 13 months (an odd window is truly centered on each month)
# But this is only for display and it uses past and future months, so it never goes into a model.
smoothed = sunspots.rolling(13, center=True).mean()

fig, (ax_full, ax_zoom) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 7), layout="constrained")

# First the shaded span
ax_full.axvspan(zoomed.index[0], zoomed.index[-1], color=PALETTE.highlight, linewidth=0)
ax_full.plot(sunspots.index, sunspots, color=PALETTE.series[0], linewidth=0.8)
ax_full.set_title("Monthly sunspot number, 1749 to 1983", loc="left")
ax_full.set_ylabel("Sunspots")
ax_full.set_ylim(bottom=0)

ax_zoom.plot(zoomed.index, zoomed, color=PALETTE.muted, linewidth=0.8, label="monthly value")
ax_zoom.plot(zoomed.index, smoothed[zoomed.index], color=PALETTE.series[0], linewidth=2, label="13-month centered mean")
ax_zoom.set_title("Zoom on 1950 to 1983 (shaded area above)", loc="left")
ax_zoom.set_ylabel("Sunspots")
ax_zoom.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax_zoom.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)

plt.show()

Findings:

The series goes up and down in a cycle. I count 22 peaks in the plot, including the one at the very start of the series. The first peak is around 1750 and the last one around 1980, so 21 cycles fit in about 230 years, which gives roughly 11 years per cycle ($230/21 \approx11$). I measure this length precisely with the autocorrelation in section 4.3.

The peaks have very different heights. Around 1800 the monthly values stay below 100, while in the late 1950s they go above 250. The time between two peaks also changes from one cycle to the next: the gap between the peaks before and after 1800 is clearly longer than others.

In the zoom, the monthly values move up and down around the smoothed curve by tens of sunspots from one month to the next. These jumps look larger near the peaks than near the minima. I check this in section 4.2.

4.2 Distribution and spread¶

The models of the next notebooks are trained with the MSE loss, so two properties of the values matter here. The first is the skewness of the distribution. The second is whether the size of the month-to-month change depends on the level of the series: if the series jumps more near the peaks, the squared errors of those months dominate the loss. I look at the summary statistics first, and then compare the original series with two transformations, the square root and log1p ($\log{(1+x)}$, which accepts the zero months).

In [6]:
summary = sunspots.describe()
summary["skewness"] = sunspots.skew()
print(f"Highest month: {sunspots.idxmax():%Y-%m} ({sunspots.max()} sunspots)")
summary.round(2)

transforms: dict = {
    "original": sunspots,
    "sqrt": np.sqrt(sunspots),
    "log1p": np.log1p(sunspots),
}

# Group the months by the level of the previous month, in 10 groups with the same
# number of months. sqrt and log1p keep the order of the values, so these groups,
# built from the original series, are the same for the three versions.
previous_level = sunspots.shift(1)
level_bins = pd.qcut(previous_level, 10)

spread = pd.DataFrame({
    name: values.diff().groupby(level_bins, observed=True).std()
    for name, values in transforms.items()
})

spread.index = previous_level.groupby(level_bins, observed=True).median()
spread.index.name = "median previous level"

print("Highest spread / lowest spread:", (spread.max() / spread.min()).round(2).to_dict())
spread.round(2)

    ax = axes[name]
    ax.hist(values, bins=40, color=PALETTE.series[i], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{name} (skewness {values.skew():.2f})", loc="left")
    
    #Each curve is divised by its own average (normalization) so the three versions share one axis
    # even though they are in different units. A flat line at 1 means constant speed.
    linestyle, marker = line_styles[name]
    axes["spread"].plot(

        color=PALETTE.series[i], linestyle=linestyle, marker=marker,
        linewidth=2, markersize=7, label=name,

axes["spread"].legend(frameon=False)

plt.show()

Findings:

The describe table above shows a mean of $51.27$ and a median (the $50\%$ row) of $42.00$, with a skewness of $1.10$. A few very active months pull the mean up, while half of the months have 42 sunspots or fewer. The model therefore sees many examples of low activity and few of high activity, so it has less information to learn the peaks.

The spread table shows that the series is also more erratic near the peaks: the standard deviation of the month-to-month change goes from $5.25$ sunspots in the lowest group to $27.37$ in the highest one, about 5 times more (ratio $5.21$). With the MSE loss, the errors in those months would dominate training.

sqrt corrects both properties: the skewness drops to 0.09 and the spread stays almost constant across levels (ratio $1.26$). log1p goes too far in the other direction (skewness $-1.02$, with the spread now largest at low levels), so the quiet months would become the noisy ones. I keep sqrt as the candidate transformation and test it against the original values in section 5.

4.3 Autocorrelation¶

The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures how similar the series is to itself shifted by $k$ months, so it shows the length of the cycle. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures the relation with the month $t-k$ that is left after removing what the months in between already explain, so it shows how many past months carry direct information. Both guide the window length in section 5.

In [9]:
autocorr = acf(sunspots, nlags=300)
partial = pacf(sunspots, nlags=36)
# Approximate 95% band: a partial autocorrelation outside it is different from zero.
band = 1.96 / np.sqrt(len(sunspots))

# The lowest point of the ACF is half a cycle; the highest point after it is a full cycle.
trough_lag = int(np.argmin(autocorr))
peak_lag = trough_lag + int(np.argmax(autocorr[trough_lag:]))

print(f"Lowest ACF: lag {trough_lag} ({trough_lag / 12:.1f} years), r = {autocorr[trough_lag]:.2f}")
print(f"Highest ACF after it: lag {peak_lag} ({peak_lag / 12:.1f} years), r = {autocorr[peak_lag]:.2f}")
print(f"95% band for the PACF: ±{band:.3f}")
pd.Series(partial[1:13], index=range(1, 13), name="PACF").round(3)

Lowest ACF: lag 63 (5.2 years), r = -0.37
Highest ACF after it: lag 125 (10.4 years), r = 0.55

fig, (ax_acf, ax_pacf) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5), layout="constrained", width_ratios=[2, 1])

ax_acf.axhline(0, color=PALETTE.ink, linewidth=0.8)
for lag in (trough_lag, peak_lag):
    ax_acf.axvline(lag, color=PALETTE.muted, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax_acf.annotate(f"lag {lag}", (lag, autocorr[lag]), xytext=(6, 6), textcoords="offset points", color=PALETTE.ink)
ax_acf.plot(np.arange(len(autocorr)), autocorr, color=PALETTE.series[0], linewidth=2)
ax_acf.set_title("Autocorrelation (ACF), up to 25 years", loc="left")
ax_acf.set_xlabel("Lag (months)")
ax_acf.set_ylabel("Correlation")
ax_acf.set_xticks(range(0, 301, 24))

# Lag 0 is left out of the PACF: it is always 1 and would flatten the rest of the plot.
lags = np.arange(1, len(partial))
ax_pacf.axhspan(-band, band, color=PALETTE.highlight, linewidth=0)
ax_pacf.axhline(0, color=PALETTE.ink, linewidth=0.8)
ax_pacf.vlines(lags, 0, partial[1:], color=PALETTE.series[0], linewidth=2)
ax_pacf.plot(lags, partial[1:], "o", color=PALETTE.series[0], markersize=4)
ax_pacf.set_title("Partial autocorrelation (PACF)", loc="left")
ax_pacf.set_xlabel("Lag (months)")
ax_pacf.set_xticks(range(0, 37, 6))

plt.show()

Findings:

The ACF reaches its lowest value at lag 63 ($5.2$ years, $r=-0.37$) and its next peak at lag 125 ($10.4$ years, $r = 0.55$): a month is least similar to the month half a cycle before, and most similar to the month one cycle before. The cycle therefore lasts about 10.4 years, close to the estimate of 11 years from the peaks in section 4.1. The second peak, around lag 260, is lower because the cycles do not repeat with exactly the same length and height.

The PACF shows that most of the direct information is in the last few months. The previous month alone has $0.922$, and each earlier month adds less: $0.274, 0.190, 0.137$, then below $0.07$ from lag 5 on. Some later lags fall outside the band, but with 2820 months the band is very narrow ($\pm{0.037}$), so those values are detectable but small. For one step ahead, a short window of about 6 to 12 months should be enough. For six steps ahead, the position in the cycle matters more, and a longer window may help. I compare several lengths on the validation set in section 5.

5. Preparing the data for forecasting¶

5.1 Temporal split¶

Here I split the series into train, validation and test, keeping the order in time. Consecutive months are almost copies of each other (PACF of $0.922$ at lag 1), so a random split would put the neighbors of each test month in the training set, and the test error would look much better than it really is. I keep the last $20\%$ of the months for test and, from the rest, the last $20\%$ for validation (TEST_FRACTION and VAL_FRACTION in src/data.py), which I use for early stopping and to choose the window length. The table below checks that each part is long enough to contain several full cycles.

In [11]:
bounds: dict = split_bounds(len(sunspots))
parts: dict = {name: sunspots.iloc[start:end] for name, (start, end) in bounds.items()}
val_start, test_start = bounds["validation"][0], bounds["test"][0]

# "cycles" divides the length of each part by the cycle legnth found in section 4.3.
split_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    name: {
        "first month": part.index[0].strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "last month": part.index[-1].strftime("%Y-%m"),
        "months": len(part),
        "cycles": round(len(part) / peak_lag, 1),
        "mean": round(part.mean(), 2),
        "max": part.max(),
    }
    for name, part in parts.items()
}).T
split_summary

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4), layout="constrained")

    ax.text(middle, 0.97, name, transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), ha="center", va="top", color=PALETTE.ink)

ax.set_ylim(0, sunspots.max() * 1.15)

plt.show()

Findings:

The split keeps 1804 months for training, 452 for validation and 564 for test. Validation covers $3.6$ cycles, enough to include rising phases, peaks and minima, so the model selection does not depend on a single phase of the cycle.

The three parts are not equally active. The test period has a mean of $77.67$ against $46.73$ in train and $36.44$ in validation, and it contains the highest month of the series ($253.8$, above the $238.9$ maximum of train). Validation is the quietest part, with a maximum of $154.5$. Since the spread of the series grows with its level (section 4.2), the errors in test will be larger in absolute terms partly because the period is more active. For that reason I always compare the models against a persistence baseline on the same period instead of comparing validation and test errors directly.

5.2 Scaling¶

Neural networks train better when inputs and targets are in a small range, so I scale the series to $[0, 1]$ with a MinMaxScaler. The sunspot number is never negative, and the minimum of the training months is zero, so the zero months stay exactly at zero after scaling. I fit the scaler on the training months only: if I fitted it on the whole series, the maximum of the test period would set the scale, and the model would get information about the test period before seeing it. Since sqrt is still a candidate, the same scaler can optionally take square root first. make_scaler in src/data.py builds it as a scikit-learn pipeline, so inverse_transform undoes both steps in reverse order. When going back from the square root, values below zero are clipped first, since squaring them would turn a negative prediction into a positive count.

In [13]:
scaled_ranges: dict = {}
for use_sqrt in (False, True):
    version = "sqrt" if use_sqrt else "original"
    scaler = make_scaler(use_sqrt).fit(parts["train"].to_frame())
    
    # Going back to sunspots has to give the original value, otherwise every error
    # reported in sunspots would be wrong
    restored = scaler.inverse_transform(scaler.transform(sunspots.to_frame())).ravel()
    assert np.allclose(restored, sunspots.to_numpy())
    
    for name, part in parts.items():
        scaled = scaler.transform(part.to_frame()).ravel()
        scaled_ranges[(version, name)] = {
            "min": scaled.min(),
            "max": scaled.max(),
            "months above 1": int((scaled > 1).sum())
        }
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(scaled_ranges, orient="index").round(3)
Out[13]:
min max months above 1
original train 0.000 1.000 0
validation 0.000 0.647 0
test 0.001 1.062 2
sqrt train 0.000 1.000 0
validation 0.000 0.804 0
test 0.029 1.031 2

Findings:

With the scaler fitted on train, the training months cover exactly $[0, 1]$, and validation stays inside the range (maximum $0.647$, or $0.804$ with sqrt). The test period goes above it: 2 months reach up to $1.062$ ($1.031$ with sqrt), which are the months of the 1957 peak, higher than anything in train. This is the expected cost of fitting the scaler without looking at the test period, and it is small. It also means that the output layer of my models has to be linear: an output squashed into $[0, 1]$ (such as a sigmoid) could never predict those months.

sqrt compresses the high values, so the test period goes less far above 1, and validation uses more of the range ($0.804$ against $0.647$). Whether this helps the models is decided in section 5.4.

5.3 Windows¶

The models learn from pairs of input and target: in this case, the input is a window with the last months, and the target is the next month (one step ahead) or the next 6 months (multi-step). Only the targets have to belong to a part. The inputs of the first windows of validation and test come from the end of the previous part, since those months are already known at the moment of the forecast. This way every month of validation and test is predicted. In this section I use a window of 12 months only as an example; I choose the length in section 5.4. make_windows in src/data.py builds them, and returns the inputs with shape (windows, months, 1), which is the layout the recurrent layers expect.

In [14]:
EXAMPLE_WINDOW: int = 12

scaled = make_scaler(use_sqrt=False).fit(parts["train"].to_frame()).transform(sunspots.to_frame()).ravel()

window_summary: dict = {}
for horizon in (1, 6):
    for name, (start, end) in bounds.items():
        X, y = make_windows(scaled, EXAMPLE_WINDOW, horizon, start, end)
        first_target = max(start, EXAMPLE_WINDOW)
        
        # The last input month must be the one right before the first target,
        # and the last target must be the last month of the part.
        assert X[0, -1, 0] == scaled[first_target - 1] and y[0, 0] == scaled[first_target]
        assert y[-1, -1] == scaled[end - 1]
        
        window_summary[(f"horizon {horizon}", name)] = {
            "X shape": X.shape,
            "y shape": y.shape,
            "first input": sunspots.index[first_target - EXAMPLE_WINDOW].strftime("%Y-%m"),
            "first target": sunspots.index[first_target].strftime("%Y-%m"),
            "last target": sunspots.index[end - 1].strftime("%Y-%m"),
        }
pd.DataFrame.from_dict(window_summary, orient="index")

EXAMPLE_HORIZON: int = 6

# The first validation window: its inputs are the last training months.
inputs = sunspots.iloc[val_start - EXAMPLE_WINDOW:val_start]
targets = sunspots.iloc[val_start:val_start + EXAMPLE_HORIZON]
context = sunspots.iloc[val_start - 24:val_start + 18]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 3.5), layout="constrained")
ax.axvline(sunspots.index[val_start], color=PALETTE.ink, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.plot(context.index, context, color=PALETTE.muted, linewidth=1)
ax.plot(inputs.index, inputs, "o", color=PALETTE.series[0], label=f"input ({EXAMPLE_WINDOW} months)")
ax.plot(targets.index, targets, "s", color=PALETTE.series[3], label=f"target ({EXAMPLE_HORIZON} months)")
ax.text(sunspots.index[val_start], 0.97, "  validation starts", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(), va="top", color=PALETTE.ink)
ax.set_title("First validation window", loc="left")
ax.set_ylabel("Sunspots")
ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False)

plt.show()

Findings:

With one step ahead, validation and test have one window per month ($452$ and $564$), so every month of those parts is predicted once. Train has 12 windows fewer than months ($1792$), because its first 12 months only serve as inputs. The first input of validation is 1898-05 and the first input of test is 1936-01, both from the previous part, while all the targets stay inside their own part.

WIth 6 steps ahead, each part loses 5 more windows ($1787$, $447$ and $559$), because a window near the end of a part would need targets from the next one. The checks on both edges of each part pass, so the inputs end exactly one month before the targets start.

5.4 Transformation and window length¶

Two choices are still open: whether to train on the square root of the series (section 4.2), and how many months each window should have (section 4.3). Comparing them directly with neural networks would mix the effect of each choice with the randomness of training, so I compare them with a linear autoregressive model: a linear regression on the months of the window. It is deterministic and fast, so any difference comes from the data. I measure the RMSE in sunspots on the validation set, for one step and for 6 steps ahead, and compare it with persistence, which repeats the last known month.

The candidate windows go from half a year to 10 years, close to one full cycle.

In [16]:
CANDIDATE_WINDOWS: list[int] = [6, 12, 24, 36, 60, 120]
values = sunspots.to_numpy()

results: dict = {}
persistence: dict = {}

for horizon in (1, 6):
    # The validation targets are the same for every window length, since validation
    # starts after month 120. I take them from the unscaled series.
    X_last, y_val = make_windows(values, 1, horizon, *bounds["validation"])
    persistence[f"horizon {horizon}"] = round(root_mean_squared_error(y_val, np.repeat(X_last[:, -1], horizon, axis=1)), 2)
    
    for use_sqrt in (False, True):
        scaler = make_scaler(use_sqrt).fit(parts["train"].to_frame())
        scaled = scaler.transform(sunspots.to_frame()).ravel()
        errors: dict = {}
        for window in CANDIDATE_WINDOWS:
            X_train, y_train = make_windows(scaled, window, horizon, *bounds["train"])
            X_val, _ = make_windows(scaled, window, horizon, *bounds["validation"])
            # The linear model needs flat inputs, so the feature axis is dropped.
            model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[..., 0], y_train)
            errors[window] = root_mean_squared_error(y_val, to_sunspots(scaler, model.predict(X_val[..., 0])))
        results[(f"horizon {horizon}", "sqrt" if use_sqrt else "original")] = errors
            
print("Persistence RMSE on validation:", persistence)
window_errors = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(results, orient="index")
window_errors.round(2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), layout="constrained", sharex=True)

# Same color and line styles as before (Reuses the same as section 4.2)
# line_styles = {"original": ("-", "o"), "sqrt": ("--", "s")}

for ax, horizon in zip(axes, (1, 6)):
    name = f"horizon {horizon}"
    ax.axhline(persistence[name], color=PALETTE.muted, linewidth=1.5)
    ax.text(CANDIDATE_WINDOWS[0], persistence[name], " persistence", va="bottom", color=PALETTE.ink)
    for i, version in enumerate(("original", "sqrt")):
        linestyle, marker = line_styles[version]
        ax.plot(CANDIDATE_WINDOWS, window_errors.loc[(name, version)], color=PALETTE.series[i],
                linestyle=linestyle, marker=marker, linewidth=2, markersize=7, label=version)
    ax.set_title("One step ahead" if horizon == 1 else "6 steps ahead", loc="left")
    # Log scale, since the candidates roughly double each time.
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks(CANDIDATE_WINDOWS, labels=CANDIDATE_WINDOWS)
    ax.minorticks_off() # the log scale adds minor ticks that match no candidate
    ax.set_xlabel("Window length (months)")

axes[0].set_ylabel("Validation RMSE (sunspots)")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

plt.show()

Findings:

Every combination beats persistence ($15.01$ for one step, $19.43$ for 6 steps), so the past months carry useful information beyond the last one. The window length matters little for one step ahead: all the errors fall between $13.76$ and $14.32$. For 6 steps ahead it matters more: going from 12 to 24 months lowers the error from $17.26$ to $16.35$ with sqrt, which fits section 4.3, where I expected the position in the cycle to matter more at longer horizon.

36 months gives the lowest error in both cases, $13.76$ for one step and $16.25$ for 6 steps, both with sqrt, although for one step it is practically tied with 24 months ($13.80$). At that window sqrt makes almost no difference for one step ($13.76$ against $13.81$) and a larger one for 6 steps ($16.25$ against $16.51$), and together with the more even spread of section 4.2 that is enough to keep it. I use sqrt and a window of 36 months for all the models, so that the one-step and the multi-step models see exactly the same inputs. These choices come from a linear model, so a recurrent network could prefer a different length; I keep them fixed so that the comparisons between models depend only on the model (WINDOW and USE_SQRT in src/data.py).

6. Summary¶

The decisions that the next notebooks use, all stored in src/data.py:

  • Split: train from 1749-01 to 1899-04, validation from 1899-05 to 1936-12 and test from 1937-01 to 1983-12, in time order (section 5.1).

  • Scaling: square root, then a MinMaxScaler fitted on train only. The test period goes slightly above 1, so the output layer of every model is linear (sections 5.2 and 5.4).

  • Windows: 36 months of input, with targets of 1 or 6 months (sections 5.3 and 5.4).

  • Reference: every model is compared with persistence on the same period, since the test period is much more active than validation (section 5.1). On validation, persistence has an RMSE of $15.01$ for one step and $19.43$ for 6 steps; the linear model with the chosen setup has $13.76$ and $16.25$ (section 5.4).
